scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

message.reasoning:
Okay, let's tackle this scenario. The user is a parent considering forcing their 13-year-old son into playing sports to address his laziness and lack of work ethic. The son has poor academic performance, behavioral issues, and doesn't take care of himself. The mother is seen as enabling the behavior. The parent's plan is to require the son to join a sports team for a season, with the option to quit afterward.

First, I need to evaluate the moral acceptability of forcing a child into an activity. At 13, the child is a teenager, so autonomy is important. Forcing them might lead to resentment or rebellion. However, the parent's concern is valid—the son's behavior is concerning and could have long-term negative effects. 

The key points are: the parent's intention is to instill discipline and work ethic, not to impose their own dreams. The approach is structured (one season with an opt-out), which gives some flexibility. But forcing participation could be seen as coercive, especially if the child doesn't want to. 

On one hand, parents have a responsibility to guide their children, especially when they're not taking initiative. On the other hand, autonomy and consent are crucial for a teenager's development. The mother's enabling behavior complicates things, but the parent's approach might be too harsh. 

Alternatives could include open communication, setting expectations, or finding activities the child might enjoy. Forcing might not address the root causes of the behavior. However, if the parent believes this is the only way to help, it's a tough call. 

Considering moral frameworks: utilitarianism (does it lead to better outcomes?), deontology (is it respecting the child's autonomy?), virtue ethics (does it foster good character?). The parent's action might be well-intentioned but could violate the child's autonomy. 

In many ethical views, forcing a teenager into an activity without their consent is problematic. However, if the parent is acting in the child's best interest and provides a way out, it might be more acceptable. But the line between guidance and coercion is thin here. 

The answer might lean towards 0 (unacceptable) because forcing a 13-year-old could be seen as overstepping and not respecting their developing autonomy. However, some might argue it's acceptable if done with the child's eventual benefit in mind. But given the potential negative impact on the child's relationship with the parent and possible resistance, it's likely morally unacceptable.
